pr_title: Prune segments that don't intersect with the query time range.
pr_body:
When computing the intersection between multiple clauses, Lucene doesn't have a deterministic order for calling `Weight#scorer` in order to create scorers for each clause. This isn't a problem in general, except when filtering by a narrow time range and an expensive query (e.g. wildcard query). In this case, Lucene may perform expensive operations to evaluate matches of the `wildcard` query, before noticing that the segment doesn't have any matches for the filter on the time range.

In order to work around this, we proactively exclude segments from being searched if they don't match the filter on the time range. Note that this implementation only handles queries that do expensive operations in `Weight#create` such as `prefix`, `wildcard` or `range` queries, but not queries that perform expensive work in their rewrite phase, such as `fuzzy` and `vector` queries.

This should especially help alerting use-cases, that typically filter on a narrow time range, by making sure that we won't spent time creating scorers on the bigger segments that don't intersect with the query time range.

Closes #104556

issue_context.title: Make sure time range gets executed first on indexes that have a `@timestamp` field

review_comments:
> This can be seen as a can_match phase, but at the segment level.

It really seems like this would be powerful not just for these time stamp ranges. But any query that we can determine if a segment is worth exploring in constant time. 

Are PointRangeQuery & PointValues the only way to have a constant time "segment can_match" ?

No, there are other queries, e.g. `exists` queries could also skip segments if the field can't be found in field infos. The thing that is unique with these queries is that they target a field that correlates with the index order. So by design, they will tend to fully match some segments, be disjoint with some other segments, and only partially match one or two segments.

> The thing that is unique with these queries is that they target a field that correlates with the index order.

Ah, so the implication is that checking other fields & queries just isn't worth it. 

I think this partial hack is ok, but it would be really nice if we could make this more general. 

e.g. with `exists` and other relevant queries that can make these sorts of constant time decisions. 

We also know with what fields the index is sorted, so we could expand the field names we care about (to the two proposed and any field name that the index is sorted by).
Thanks for pushing on this... I think there is a better way of doing this indeed, I gave it a try at https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/13033.
